name: French
modelReview: built 2026-11-12 by Claude Fable 5.2 from the questionnaire answers, lexicon and visible paradigms, after two schedule reads and three blind fluency reads of the rows; 153 of 153 held-out rows pass on the first judged run, after a tie rule the builder stopped on was added to the rule book (tooling/experiments/renderer-process/fr-acceptance.md); audited 2026-11-13 by Claude Fable 5.2 (an adversarial read of the rule book, the renderer and about 3,000 sentences against their fire times), which repaired a wrong day for a count from the end of February, exceptions that took away a moment a window named, runs wrapped the long way round, and lists of seconds nobody could hold; audited a second time 2026-11-13 by Claude Fable 5.2 with the core's calendar facts, a list of traps from eight languages and usage notes written in French (usage.md): a pattern that never fires or fires only in leap years now says so, months a day cannot fire in are not named, years with no end and sets of runs and cadences are no longer lists, and no word for a working day is used (a date that falls on a Saturday or a Sunday moves to the Friday or the Monday); none of the second audit's forms has had a blind fluency read, and no fluent human has read the result; 2026-11-13: says when both day fields must match (a day field written from a star beside a restricted one, as in Vixie cron), in rows, rule and renderer written by Claude Sonnet 5.5 from this rule book's seed and reviewed by Claude Fable 5.2; a blind Sonnet reader told these sentences from the union's 16 times of 16, and none has had a blind fluency read; 2026-11-14, on the maintainer's rulings, by Claude Opus 5.5: an hour cadence that tiles the day is said bare (« toutes les 2 heures », with no window, list or « tous les jours ») or from its start (« toutes les 2 heures à partir de 1 h »), with a tiling cadence missing some hours said as that cadence « sauf »; a cadence that does not tile keeps both ends; minutes beside such hours are said apart (« à la minute 30, toutes les 2 heures ») and minutes that fill the hour sweep « une heure sur deux »; a minute against the hour is « à la minute 30 de chaque heure » or « aux minutes 5, 25 et 45 de chaque heure », unpadded, in every form that names one (stretches, exceptions, strays, offsets); the rule book was amended first and every affected row rewritten by hand before the renderer changed; there were no brackets of number series to remove; nothing was blind-read, and no fluent human has read the new forms; 2026-11-14, also by Claude Opus 5.5: where no clock time carries the first second, two to six seconds that are no run are named (« à la minute 30 de chaque heure, aux secondes 17, 28, 39 et 50 ») instead of an offset, a step and a length; rule book first, rows by hand, then the renderer; not blind-read; then, by the same hand the same day: beside a clock time too, such seconds are named after the time said to the minute (« tous les jours à 9 h, aux secondes 17, 28, 39 et 50 »), and a run of seconds off the top of the minute is a stretch (« toutes les secondes de la seconde 17 à la seconde 20 »); rows by hand first; not blind-read; 2026-11-14, released stable on the full reading check: all 754 rows read by three Sonnet 5.5 readers briefed only in the language (5395 questions about moments, scored against an answer key that shares no code with the library), and each of the 14 questions most readers got wrong asked again alone of three Sonnet 5.5 and three Opus 5.5 readers: none was still misread by most readers of both (tooling/scripts/reading/recheck.mjs); 2026-11-19, by Claude Opus 5.5: every second day that runs to the end of the longest month it fires in is the idiom alone however the field is written (`1-29/2` in June is « les jours impairs de juin », as `*/2` is), because one set of days was said two ways; rule first, rows by hand, then the renderer from the core's `daysReached`
